Answer with the JSON object {"mechanism": str (why the feature should predict next week's relative return across sectors), "rationale": str (why it is not already captured by the six features), "feature_idea": str (how to compute it from weekly closes, the S&P 500 and the market states)}.

request.system: You are a quantitative researcher in a small research lab. The lab studies a weekly strategy that ranks 9 anonymised US sector ETFs (codes A1 to A9) after each Friday close; the top 2 are bought and the bottom 2 sold the next Monday, with a market hedge. A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday. Your job is to propose ONE new feature with an economic mechanism that could improve the cross-sectional ranking beyond these six. Features are computed only from past weekly prices, so they cannot use the future. You never trade and you never see raw prices. Always answer with one JSON object.

response: {"mechanism": "Nearness to the 52-week high of a sector's market-relative price (George & Hwang anchoring effect). Investors anchor on the 52-week high as a reference point and are reluctant to push prices through it, so sectors trading close to their relative 52-week high tend to continue drifting up as news gets absorbed slowly, while sectors far below their high have already been de-anchored and show weaker continuation. Computing it on the sector-to-SPY ratio isolates the relative-strength anchor that matters for a market-hedged long-short book, so the signal predicts next week's cross-sectional relative return rather than market direction.", "rationale": "DD13 measures drawdown only over 13 weeks of raw total-return closes, so it is dominated by recent market swings and short noise; MOM26_1 and MOM52_4 measure point-to-point returns, which George & Hwang show is a different (and weaker) summary of the price path than the distance to the long-horizon high. A sector can have strong 12-month momentum yet sit well below its relative high after a recent slide, or weak momentum yet be pinned at a new relative high after a long base. Using the close/SPY ratio also strips out the common market component that leaks into DD13 and momentum, so the new feature should have only moderate correlation with the existing six (expected 0.3-0.5 with MOM52_4/DD13, near zero with VOL13/BETA52/REV1).", "feature_idea": "Relative price rel(t) = close(t)/spy(t). Feature = log( rel(t) / max(rel(t-51..t)) ), i.e. the log distance of the sector's market-relative price from its 52-week relative high (always <= 0, 0 = at the high). Then cs_z across the 9 sectors each Friday. DSL: {\"name\":\"REL52HIGH\",\"expr\":{\"op\":\"cs_z\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"input\":\"close\"},\"b\":{\"input\":\"spy\"}},\"b\":{\"op\":\"rolling\",\"stat\":\"max\",\"n\":52,\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"input\":\"close\"},\"b\":{\"input\":\"spy\"}}}}}}} (11 nodes, depth 5). Higher values (closer to the relative 52-week high) are expected to rank higher for next week's relative return. Optional variant: wrap the cs_z root in mul_state with BEAR24 complement is not available, so keep it unscaled; if desired, test a lag-1 version of rel in the numerator to remove any overlap with REV1."}

messages.content:
Feature idea: {"feature_idea":"Compute weekly log returns of the sector and SPY (diff n=1 of log close). Build a 17-week rolling mean of SPY returns; isolate down-week indicator-like weight by comparing current SPY return to 0 via a ratio of {diff log close sector, diff log close spy} multiplied by a state where market return is negative. Concretely: downside_capture = cs_z( ratio( rolling mean n=17 of (diff log sector return), rolling mean n=17 of (diff log spy return) , restricted to negative SPY weeks ) ). Implement directly as cs_z( ratio( rolling_mean_17( diff_log_close ), rolling_mean_17( diff_log_spy ) ) ) using the spy leaf, then multiply by market state BEAR24 at the root to concentrate the defensive-rotation signal in market-stress regimes.","mechanism":"Sectors that have recently moved in opposite direction to the market (negative rolling beta/high idiosyncratic resilience during market down-weeks) should earn a relative-return premium next week: when the market wobbles, low-sensitivity sectors attract defensive flows and are less exposed to transient market drawdowns. Computing a short-window (13-17 week) downside-capture ratio isolates the asymmetric co-movement that a single full-sample beta cannot express.","rationale":"BETA52 is a 52-week (≈126-day) level beta and VOL13 is total volatility, both dominated by the unconditional co-movement level and highly collinear (BETA52-VOL13 correlation 0.96). Neither isolates asymmetric downside co-movement over a short recent window. A downside-capture ratio uses only weeks when SPY fell and normalises sector return by SPY return, capturing conditional beta on down moves rather than overall volatility or level beta. MOM and REV capture the sector's own past return, not its sensitivity to market downside, so the signal is economically distinct and orthogonal to the current six in the relevant tail state."}

Translate the feature idea into exactly one spec of the DSL. Use only the operations listed. Answer with the JSON object {"spec": {"name": str, "expr": node}}.

request.system: You translate feature ideas into a JSON feature DSL. Feature DSL (JSON, no code). A spec is {"name": str, "expr": node}. Leaves: {"input": "close"} (the sector's weekly close, a total-return index) and {"input": "spy"} (the S&P 500's weekly close, the same for every sector). Operations, every window ending at the current week t, n in weeks: {"op": "lag", "n": 1-104, "x": node}; {"op": "rolling", "stat": "mean"|"std"|"sum"|"min"|"max", "n": 2-104, "x": node}; {"op": "diff", "n": 1-104, "x": node} (x(t) - x(t-n)); {"op": "log", "x": node}; {"op": "ratio", "a": node, "b": node}; {"op": "cs_z", "x": node} and {"op": "cs_rank", "x": node} (z-score or rank across the 9 sectors each week); {"op": "mul_state", "state": S or [S1, S2], "x": node} with S in BEAR24 (1 after a negative 2-year market return, else 0), MKT_VAR (126-day market variance), VIX, TERM (10y-3m yield spread), CREDIT (BAA-10y spread). Rules: the root must be cs_z or cs_rank, or mul_state whose child is cs_z or cs_rank; mul_state only at the root (a market state alone cannot reorder sectors, so it can only scale a cross-sectional feature); at most 25 nodes and depth 10. Example, the weekly log return: {"op": "diff", "n": 1, "x": {"op": "log", "x": {"input": "close"}}}.

request.system: You are a quantitative researcher in a small research lab. The lab studies a weekly strategy that ranks 9 anonymised US sector ETFs (codes A1 to A9) after each Friday close; the top 2 are bought and the bottom 2 sold the next Monday, with a market hedge. A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday. Your job is to propose ONE new feature with an economic mechanism that could improve the cross-sectional ranking beyond these six. Features are computed only from past weekly prices, so they cannot use the future. You never trade and you never see raw prices. Always answer with one JSON object.

response: {"mechanism": "Volatility surprise: a sector whose recent (4-week) realised volatility is high relative to its own 26-week norm is experiencing a sector-specific information shock (earnings cluster, regulatory news, commodity move, fund flows). Such shocks are followed by elevated uncertainty, de-risking by vol-targeting and risk-parity holders, and wider spreads, which on average depresses the sector's return over the following weeks relative to sectors trading in their normal volatility regime; conversely, sectors whose volatility has collapsed below their norm tend to attract flows and drift up. The effect should be strongest when market-wide uncertainty is high, so the feature can be scaled by VIX.", "rationale": "VOL13 and BETA52 are almost the same signal (correlation 0.96) and both rank sectors by their static type (high-beta cyclicals vs defensives); they say nothing about whether a sector's volatility is unusual for that sector. Normalising short-run volatility by the sector's own longer-run volatility removes the static level and isolates the change in risk, which is nearly orthogonal to level features. It is also distinct from DD13/REV1 (which are about price level/path, not dispersion) and from the momentum features, since a volatility spike can occur on either up or down moves.", "feature_idea": "Weekly log return r = diff(1, log(close)). Compute short-run realised vol s4 = rolling std of r over 4 weeks and long-run vol s26 = rolling std of r over 26 weeks (both ending at week t). Feature = log(s4 / s26), i.e. the log volatility ratio, then z-score across the 9 sectors each Friday (cs_z). Optionally scale by the VIX market state (mul_state VIX at the root) so that the cross-sectional vol-surprise signal gets more weight when aggregate uncertainty is high. DSL: {\"name\":\"VOLSURPRISE_4_26\",\"expr\":{\"op\":\"cs_z\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"op\":\"rolling\",\"stat\":\"std\",\"n\":4,\"x\":{\"op\":\"diff\",\"n\":1,\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"input\":\"close\"}}}},\"b\":{\"op\":\"rolling\",\"stat\":\"std\",\"n\":26,\"x\":{\"op\":\"diff\",\"n\":1,\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"input\":\"close\"}}}}}}}}. Expected sign: negative (volatility spikes predict relative underperformance), but let the ranking model learn it."}
